exampleAnswers.title: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R

question.text:
\[ \bbox[5px, border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}} \, \mathbf{x} = Q^T \, \bbox[5px, border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}} \]

Let $A=QR$ be a QR decomposition of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
question.explanation:
The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the normal equation

\[ A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b}. \]

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} A^T A \mathbf{x} &= A^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] (QR)^T QR \mathbf{x} &= (QR)^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] R^T (Q^T Q) R \mathbf{x} &= R^T Q^T \mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, $Q^T Q = I,$ and we get

\[ R^T R \mathbf{x} = R^T \! Q^T \mathbf{b}. \]

Finally, since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

\begin{align*} (R^T)^{-1} \cdot R^T R \mathbf{x} &= (R^T)^{-1} \cdot R^T Q^T \mathbf{b} \\[3pt] \bbox[5px, border: 1px solid black]{\, R\, }\,\, \mathbf{x} &= Q^T \,\, \bbox[5px, border: 1px solid black]{\,\mathbf{b}\,}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are $R$ and $\mathbf{b}.$

\[ A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b}. \]

\begin{align*} A^T A \mathbf{x} &= A^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] (QR)^T QR \mathbf{x} &= (QR)^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] R^T (Q^T Q) R \mathbf{x} &= R^T Q^T \mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, $Q^T Q = I,$ and we get

\[ R^T R \mathbf{x} = R^T \! Q^T \mathbf{b}. \]

question.text: Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where \[ Q = \dfrac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad R = \dfrac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 6 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

\[ A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b} \]

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} A^T A \mathbf{x} &= A^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] (QR)^T QR \mathbf{x} &= (QR)^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] R^T (Q^T Q) R \mathbf{x} &= R^T Q^T \mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, $Q^T Q = I,$ and we get

\[ R^T R \mathbf{x} = R^T \! Q^T \mathbf{b}. \]

Finally, since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

\begin{align*} (R^T)^{-1} \cdot R^T R \mathbf{x} &= (R^T)^{-1} \cdot R^T Q^T \mathbf{b} \\[3pt] R \mathbf{x} &= Q^T \mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

\begin{align*} \overbrace{\dfrac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}}^{\large R} \mathbf{x} &= \overbrace{\dfrac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}}^{\large Q^T} \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 6 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}}^{\large \mathbf{b}} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x} &= \begin{bmatrix} 33 \\ -6 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

which gives the system

\[ \begin{cases} 3x_1 - 5 x_2 = 33 \\ 2 x_2 = -6. \end{cases} \]

From the second equation, we get $x_2=-3.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

\begin{align*} 3x_1 - 5 (-3) &= 33 \\[3pt] 3x_1 &= 18 \\[3pt] x_1 &= 6. \end{align*}

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is $\begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}.$

example.title: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given a QR Factorization

question.text: Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where \[ Q = \dfrac{1}{25} \begin{bmatrix} -7 & 24 \\ -24 & -7 \end{bmatrix}, \quad R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 5\\ 10 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

\[ A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b} \]

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} A^T A \mathbf{x} &= A^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] (QR)^T QR \mathbf{x} &= (QR)^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] R^T (Q^T Q) R \mathbf{x} &= R^T Q^T \mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Since $Q$ is orthogonal, $Q^T Q = I,$ and we get

\[ R^T R \mathbf{x} = R^T \! Q^T \mathbf{b}. \]

Finally, since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

\begin{align*} (R^T)^{-1} \cdot R^T R \mathbf{x} &= (R^T)^{-1} \cdot R^T Q^T \mathbf{b} \\[3pt] R \mathbf{x} &= Q^T \mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

\begin{align*} \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{\large R} \mathbf{x} &= \overbrace{\dfrac{1}{25} \begin{bmatrix} -7 & -24 \\ 24 & -7 \end{bmatrix}}^{\large Q^T} \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix}}^{\large \mathbf{b}} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x} &= \begin{bmatrix} -11 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

which gives the system

\[ \begin{cases} x_1 - x_2 = -11\\ x_2 = 2. \end{cases} \]

From the second equation, we get $x_2=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

\begin{align*} x_1 - (2) &= -11 \\[3pt] x_1 &= -9. \end{align*}

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is $\begin{bmatrix} -9 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$

question.text: Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where \[ Q = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{70}}\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt 5 & \sqrt 2 \\ 3\sqrt 5 & 3\sqrt 2 \\ 2\sqrt 5 & -5\sqrt 2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad R = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{70}} \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

\[ A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b} \]

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} A^T A \mathbf{x} &= A^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] (QR)^T QR \mathbf{x} &= (QR)^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] R^T (Q^T Q) R \mathbf{x} &= R^T Q^T \mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, $Q^T Q = I,$ and we get

\[ R^T R \mathbf{x} = R^T \! Q^T \mathbf{b}. \]

Finally, since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

\begin{align*} (R^T)^{-1} \cdot R^T R \mathbf{x} &= (R^T)^{-1} \cdot R^T Q^T \mathbf{b} \\[3pt] R \mathbf{x} &= Q^T \mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

\begin{align*} \overbrace{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{70}} \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt 2 \end{bmatrix}}^{\large R} \mathbf{x} &= \overbrace{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{70}}\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{5} & 3\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt 2 & 3\sqrt 2 & -5\sqrt 2 \end{bmatrix}}^{\large Q^T} \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}^{\large \mathbf{b}} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt 2 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x} &= \begin{bmatrix} -10\sqrt{5} \\ -10\sqrt 2 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

which gives the system

\[ \begin{cases} \sqrt{5}x_1 + 2\sqrt{5} x_2 = -10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt2 x_2 = -10\sqrt 2. \end{cases} \]

From the second equation, we get $x_2=-10.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

\begin{align*} \sqrt{5}x_1 + 2\sqrt{5} (-10) &= -10\sqrt{5} \\[3pt] \sqrt{5}x_1 &= 10\sqrt{5} \\[3pt] x_1 &= 10. \end{align*}

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is $\begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ -10 \end{bmatrix}.$

question.text: Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where \[ Q = \dfrac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix} 8 & -1 \\ 4 & 4 \\ -1 & 8 \end{bmatrix}, \quad R = \dfrac{1}{9} \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
The least-squares solution $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

\[ A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T \mathbf{b} \]

Substituting $A = QR,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} A^T A \mathbf{x} &= A^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] (QR)^T QR \mathbf{x} &= (QR)^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] R^T (Q^T Q) R \mathbf{x} &= R^T Q^T \mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, $Q^T Q = I,$ and we get

\[ R^TR\mathbf{x} = R^TQ^T \mathbf{b}. \]

Finally, since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

\begin{align*} (R^T)^{-1} \cdot R^T R \mathbf{x} &= (R^T)^{-1} \cdot R^T Q^T \mathbf{b} \\[3pt] R \mathbf{x} &= Q^T \mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

\begin{align*} \overbrace{\dfrac{1}{9} \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{\large R} \mathbf{x} &= \overbrace{\dfrac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix} 8 & 4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix}}^{\large Q^T} \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{\large \mathbf{b}} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x} &= \begin{bmatrix} -9 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

which gives the system

\[ \begin{cases} 9x_1 + 8 x_2 = -9 \\ x_2 = 9. \end{cases} \]

From the second equation, we get $x_2 = 9.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

\begin{align*} 9x_1 + 8(9) &= -9 \\[3pt] 9x_1 &= -81 \\[3pt] x_1 &= -9. \end{align*}

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is $\begin{bmatrix} -9 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix}.$

question.text: Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where \[ Q = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & \sqrt{2} \\ 2 & -\sqrt{2} \\ 1 & \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}, \quad R = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 8 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

\[ A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b} \]

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} A^T A \mathbf{x} &= A^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] (QR)^T QR \mathbf{x} &= (QR)^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] R^T (Q^T Q) R \mathbf{x} &= R^T Q^T \mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, $Q^T Q = I,$ and we get

\[ R^T R \mathbf{x} = R^T \! Q^T \mathbf{b}. \]

Finally, since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

\begin{align*} (R^T)^{-1} \cdot R^T R \mathbf{x} &= (R^T)^{-1} \cdot R^T Q^T \mathbf{b} \\[3pt] R \mathbf{x} &= Q^T \mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

\begin{align*} \overbrace{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}}^{\large R} \mathbf{x} &= \overbrace{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ \sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}}^{\large Q^T} \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 8 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}}^{\large \mathbf{b}} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt2 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x} &= \begin{bmatrix} 20 \\ -4\sqrt2 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

which gives the system

\[ \begin{cases} 2x_1 - x_2 = 20 \\ 2\sqrt2 x_2 = -4\sqrt2. \end{cases} \]

From the second equation, we get $x_2=-2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

\begin{align*} 2x_1 - (-2) &= 20 \\[3pt] 2x_1 &= 18 \\[3pt] x_1 &= 9. \end{align*}

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is $\begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}.$
